analysis.one_liner: Repeals the fracking exemption in the Safe Drinking Water Act and requires disclosure of fracking chemicals.
analysis.headline: The bill never left committee: it was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and its Environment Subcommittee in July 2019 and no vote was ever taken before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Since 2005, the Safe Drinking Water Act has excluded hydraulic fracturing from the underground injection rules that otherwise apply when fluids are pumped deep into the ground. This bill would delete that exclusion, putting fracking operations under EPA and state drinking-water protection for groundwater, and would require companies to list the chemicals they plan to inject and the chemicals actually used, posted publicly online. In medical emergencies, companies would have to hand over proprietary chemical formulas to treating doctors or nurses without waiting for paperwork.
analysis.who_benefits: People who live near fracking operations and drink well water or rely on groundwater would gain federal protection against pollution from the fluids pumped into fracked wells, and would be able to look up which chemicals were used at sites near them. Emergency medical workers would gain the right to learn, on the spot, what a patient exposed to fracking fluids was injected with.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Residents near fracking sites and their doctors

how_it_helps.text: Deletes the Safe Drinking Water Act exclusion for hydraulic fracturing, so underground injection of fracking fluids counts as regulated injection under the Act [S3].
Gives the EPA authority to protect groundwater sources such as wells from pollution risks posed by fracking operations [S2].

Requires companies to disclose, before fracking begins and within 30 days after it ends, the chemicals injected, their identities and volumes, with the information posted publicly on the internet [S3].

In a medical emergency, companies must immediately disclose proprietary chemical formulas to the state, the EPA, or the treating physician or nurse, without requiring a written statement of need or a confidentiality agreement first [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Oil and gas drilling companies would bear the cost of complying with drinking-water permitting for fracking wells and of tracking and disclosing chemical use, including giving up some trade-secret protection during emergencies.

drawbacks.text: The bill subjects every fracked well to underground injection permitting, a process the industry argues could add cost and delay to a drilling method responsible for a large share of U.S. oil and gas production; slower or costlier drilling can show up in higher energy prices [S3].

The disclosure rules give states and the EPA wide discretion over what counts as compliance, and the bill leaves the details to later regulations, so the real-world burden is unknown until rules are written [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public benefit is direct: federal groundwater protection and public chemical disclosure for a practice currently exempt from them, plus faster access to chemical identities when someone is exposed. The cost falls on drillers and potentially on energy prices. The bill is broadly drawn and leaves key details to future regulation, but its core trade is clear: tighter water protection and transparency in exchange for higher compliance costs in oil and gas production.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the Energy and Commerce Committee and its Environment Subcommittee in July 2019 and sat there without a hearing, markup, or floor vote for the rest of the two-year Congress.

narrative.text: Rep. Diana DeGette introduced the bill on July 25, 2019, joined by 24 other House members as original cosponsors [S1].
The House referred it to the Committee on Energy and Commerce on July 25, 2019 [S5].
The next day it was referred to the Subcommittee on Environment and Climate Change [S5].
No further action was taken: the bill never received a committee vote or a floor vote before the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil and gas companies kept the Safe Drinking Water Act exemption for fracking and faced no federal chemical-disclosure requirement. Residents near fracking sites remained without the groundwater protections the bill would have provided.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Oil and gas drillers kept their exemption

against.what_they_did: Received the referral on July 25, 2019 and took no further action; no hearing, markup, or vote was ever recorded on the bill [S5].

sides.party_line_note: All 26 cosponsors and the sponsor were Democrats; no Republican supported the bill, and the Democratic-controlled committee never moved it.

industries.note: The bill would end the industry's 2005 exemption from Safe Drinking Water Act underground injection rules and force public disclosure of injected chemicals, including trade-secret formulas in emergencies. Because the industry's interest is in keeping drilling cheap and chemical formulas confidential while the public's interest is in protected groundwater, the two run against each other in this bill.

industries.industry: Groundwater-dependent communities and rural water users
industries.note: Not an industry, but the bill's regulated parties exist to protect these people: they would gain enforceable federal groundwater protections and public chemical disclosures for nearby fracking operations.
